To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the force deficit and percentage of damaged muscle fiber were similar in the vitamin E-treated and control rats.
vitamin E treatment does not ameliorate the force deficit or the percentage of damaged fibers after a protocol of lengthening contractions in rat muscles.

1) a single bout of eccentric contractions causes a significant loss in force and a significant increase in the number of damaged muscle fibers; 2) the loss in force and the percentage of muscle fibers damaged are not ameliorated by vitamin E treatment; 3) the serum activities of the enzymes pyruvate and creatine kinase are elevated after eccentric contractions, but the elevation is not ameliorated with vitamin E treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of vitamin C and E in the prevention and treatment of muscle injuries.
the mechanism of contraction-induced muscle injury.
the mechanisms of injury induced by pliometric (stretching) contractions and the possible role of vitamin E as a therapeutic agent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the vitamin E content in muscle is not related to the extent of injury or the severity of secondary injury.
vitamin E does not prevent the induction of muscle damage but may be important in the prevention of the secondary loss of enzyme activity.
vitamin E did not protect against muscle injury induced by pliometric contractions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although vitamin E treatment was not beneficial in the prevention of the force deficit or the percentage of damaged fibers, it may have been beneficial in preventing enzyme leakage.
the antioxidant function of vitamin E is unlikely to play a role in the prevention of contraction-induced muscle injury.
the role for vitamin E after muscle injury is not as a scavenger of free radicals but rather as an antioxidant for membrane-bound enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, despite its antioxidant properties, vitamin E is not protective against muscle damage.
vitamin E supplementation did not amelioration contraction-induced muscle injury in rats.
the role of vitamin C and vitamin E in muscle damage is still an open question.
